newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK money supply shows blossoming economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK money supply shows blossoming economy.

text.p: Britain's M4 money supply growth shot up to 9.4 percent in the year to August, the Bank of England said on Thursday, and consumer credit continued to increase.

Economists said the sharp 9.4 percent pick-up in broad money growth, above the government's three-to-nine percent monitoring range, showed Britain's economy was steaming ahead and suggested interest rates should head up not down.

Figures from the British Bankers' Association showed consumer credit rose by 453 million pounds ($706.1 million) in August, down from July's 556 million increase but well above the recent monthly average of 405 million.
"All the data now are pointing to very firm economic recovery," said Jonathan Griggs, economist at Barclays Bank.

"The UK will look like one of the strongest economies in the world as we go into the pre-election countdown and I think the bias in interest rate markets has to increasingly shift towards...a pre-emptive hike."

Thursday's figures came just a day after August retail sales were shown to have leapt 1.0 percent, taking the three-month rate of growth to its strongest level in eight years and reviving memories of the late 1980s boom.

Griggs supported the line taken by Bank of England Governor Eddie George. Minutes of the July 30 meeting with Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke showed George wished to see official interest rates at 6.00 percent, not 5.75.
In those minutes George said money supply growth, often seen as a harbinger of future inflationary pressure, was consistent with rising demand growth this year and next.

The UK Treasury said the growth in August M4 was in part due to special factors, particularly the takeover of the National & Provincial building society by British bank Abbey National and subsequent payouts made to N&P account holders.
But economists said the N&P takeover was offset by a fall in gilt repos included in M4.

They said the bounce in M4 growth, after it's tumble to 9.0 percent in July, merely confirmed what most UK data have been singing from the rooftops -- Britain's economy is growing fast as consumers queue up to spend.
"The overall tone of the data is firm enough to keep the Bank of England convinced that base rates should be six percent and not 5.75," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.

But he added that there was little chance of that in the near future. With elections to be held by May 1997 and the ruling Conservative government trailing badly in opinion polls, Clarke will come under intense political pressure to boost his party's flagging fortunes.
That could involve rate cuts and/or tax cuts at the November budget.
Figures released by the Building Societies Association (BSA) at the same time as M4 showed Britain's housing market, a key part of the economy's recovery, continues to prosper.
Although new mortgage approvals fell slightly to about 3.6 billion pounds in August, the underlying trend remains powerfully upwards.

BSA director-general said gross advances on a seasonally adjusted basis were down only a little on July, signalling the strongest performance since 1990. Moreover, the N&P merger with Abbey National meant mortgage lending by N&P was now included in bank figures, not the BSA data.

"These figures provide the clearest indication that the housing market is returning to health, with the stronger than expected levels of lending over the summer period pointing to further improvements for the rest of the year," he said.
